opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the basic way to think about it is just counting the OOMs. If you look at the jump from GPT-2 to GPT-4, that was roughly preschooler to smart high schooler, and it came from something like four and a half to six orders of magnitude of effective compute. That's raw compute scaling, maybe half an order of magnitude a year from the giant buildouts, plus algorithmic efficiencies, which have been running at roughly another half OOM a year. And then on top of that, this thing I call unhobbling.

If you just extrapolate the trend lines, and I think people should take the trend lines seriously because they've been incredibly consistent, you get another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jump by around 2027. Another preschooler-to-high-schooler qualitative leap, but starting from where we are now.

The unhobbling part is what I think people underrate. Right now these models are incredibly smart in some ways but hobbled in really dumb ways. Imagine a brilliant new hire who shows up and you give them five minutes, no context about your company, no ability to use their computer properly, and they have to answer immediately without thinking. That's kind of how we've been using these models. Things like RLHF, chain of thought, tools, longer context, and test-time compute, where the model actually gets to think for hours and work through a problem, unlock huge amounts of latent capability.

So by 2027–2028 I expect we go from chatbot to something more like a drop-in remote worker. An agent that onboards like a new employee, reads your Slack and your codebase, and goes off and does a week's worth of work on a project. And once you have that, especially for AI research itself, you have to take seriously that you can run hundreds of thousands or millions of copies of automated AI researchers. That's when things could get really wild, because you might compress a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less. That's the path from AGI to superintelligence, and I think it's plausible this decade. Not certain, but plausible enough that we should be acting like it.

r001.rationale: The response extrapolates the scaling trend lines to predict another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized leap by around 2027, then discusses unhobbling as an additional source of capability.

r002.rationale: It predicts that by 2027–2028 models could move from chatbots to drop-in remote workers that onboard and complete a week's worth of project work.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is you count the orders of magnitude. If you look at what happened from GPT-2 to GPT-4, that was about four years, and we went from a model that could barely string together a coherent paragraph, kind of a preschooler, to something that's a smart high schooler, maybe passing the bar exam, writing code. And the question is, what drove that? It was three things. Compute, where we went up something like three to four orders of magnitude on training compute. Algorithmic efficiency, which people underrate, but which has been roughly another half an order of magnitude a year, so another few OOMs over that period. And then what I call unhobbling, which is taking a raw base model and making it actually useful: RLHF, chain of thought, tool use, longer context. Those don't show up neatly on a scaling plot but they're enormous.

And so the question for 2027 is just, do the trendlines continue? I think they basically do. On compute, the clusters are being built. You go from the GPT-4 cluster, which was tens of thousands of GPUs, to clusters in the hundreds of thousands, to the gigawatt and ten gigawatt clusters that are getting planned right now. That's another few OOMs of effective compute. Algorithmic progress keeps going, and if anything the labs are pouring more talent into it than ever. So by 2027, you're looking at a GPT-2 to GPT-4 sized jump again, in terms of raw scaling.

But the unhobbling piece is what I think matters most for what it actually feels like. Right now, these models are basically a very smart intern that you have to hand a single task to, who can't remember anything from yesterday, who can't use your computer, who can't go off and work for a week on something. That's not because they're not smart enough. It's because they're hobbled. The step from chatbot to agent, something that can take a task, use a browser and a terminal, work on it for hours or days, check its own work, come back to you, that is, to me, the thing that flips the switch. And I think a lot of that is going to get solved over the next couple of years because it's just so economically valuable that every lab is throwing everything at it.

So you put those together, another GPT-2 to GPT-4 jump on raw intelligence, plus the unhobbling from chatbot to drop-in remote worker, and what you get by 2027 or 2028 is something that looks a lot like an automated AI researcher. Not necessarily a genius, but a model that can do the work of a smart engineer at a lab, and you can run millions of copies of it, and they run at ten or a hundred times human speed. And that's where it gets really wild, because at that point the thing is automating the very process that made it better. That's the intelligence explosion dynamic. I think people are vastly underpricing how fast that can go once you have the automated researcher.

I'll say, the error bars are real. Maybe data runs out, maybe the unhobbling is harder than I think, maybe there's a wall on the algorithmic side. But when I look at the people who said scaling would stall at GPT-3, or GPT-4, they've been wrong every time. The trendlines have been remarkably consistent, and the plan the labs are executing is just to keep going. So my central expectation is that by 2027 we have something that is genuinely a drop-in remote worker, and shortly after that it's doing the AI research itself.

r001.rationale: It predicts another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jump by 2027 in raw scaling, before adding the separate effects of unhobbling.

r002.rationale: It predicts that unhobbling will turn chatbots into agents that can work independently for hours or days, describing the result as a drop-in remote worker.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at two things together. One is scaling: bigger training runs, better algorithms, and the resulting improvements in the underlying models. The other is what I call unhobbling—giving those models the ability to actually use their intelligence effectively.

Right now, there’s a big gap between answering a question in a chat window and doing someone’s job. Doing a job requires understanding the context, using tools, working through a problem over time, checking your work, and recovering when something goes wrong. You can have a very smart model that’s still surprisingly limited because that surrounding machinery isn’t there.

So by 2027 or 2028, I’d expect progress on both fronts to reinforce each other. You get a smarter underlying model, and then you give it the ability to work autonomously for longer stretches. The relevant question becomes less, ‘Can it produce a good answer?’ and more, ‘Can I give it a project and come back to something useful?’

The particularly consequential case is AI research. If these systems can help automate the work of improving AI itself, that creates a feedback loop: better models accelerate research, which produces better models. That doesn’t mean everything happens instantaneously. Reliability, experiments, and compute can still be bottlenecks. But I think the possibility of going from a useful assistant to something much closer to a remote worker—and eventually an AI researcher—is what makes that period so important.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling as making models smarter, but does not predict a gain beyond GPT-4 comparable to the GPT-2-to-GPT-4 gain.

r002.rationale: It predicts systems could become much closer to remote workers, but does not clearly say they would function as drop-in remote workers.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect a pretty dramatic change, though the exact timing is uncertain. There are two things happening at once: we’re scaling the underlying models, and we’re figuring out how to let them use their capabilities more effectively.

Scaling means more compute, better algorithms, and better training data. Unhobbling means things like giving a model tools, memory, and the ability to work through a problem over many steps. A system that can only give you an immediate answer is very different from one that can write code, run it, inspect the results, and keep working.

By 2027–2028, I think it’s plausible that those improvements produce systems that can do substantial portions of intellectual work autonomously. The big question is reliability: can they carry out a project over hours or days, recognize when they’re going wrong, and recover without constant human intervention?

The particularly consequential case is AI research itself. If these systems can meaningfully accelerate the development of the next generation, then the rate of progress could change. That’s why I’d be cautious about extrapolating from today’s experience of chatting with a model. The relevant comparison is what happens when you can delegate an entire task.

r001.rationale: It discusses scaling together with unhobbling, but gives no prediction about scaling alone and no comparison to the GPT-2-to-GPT-4 capability gain.

r002.rationale: It predicts autonomous work on substantial portions of intellectual tasks and possible delegation of whole tasks, but does not clearly predict that unhobbling will make scaled models function as drop-in remote workers.
